questions.question_stem: A museum issues NFTs that it says represent ownership of physical artworks. Which analysis best follows the lesson's on-chain/off-chain boundary?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum can record token ownership and transfers, but legal ownership of the physical artwork depends on off-chain agreements and institutions.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum can enforce physical asset possession rules, but authenticating the physical artwork's history requires centralized oracle certification.
Ethereum can guarantee the artwork's physical condition, but determining the current legal owner relies on sovereign courts and property registries.
Ethereum can validate the creator's real-world identity, but enforcing the transfer of custody depends on cryptographic multi-signature approvals.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames tokens as programmable claims on a shared ledger. The chain can enforce ownership of the token and contract state, but the meaning attached to that token requires off-chain legal, social, or institutional support.

questions.question_stem: A game wants one contract to manage a fungible in-game currency, many identical consumable items, and several unique character skins. Which standard best fits that design pressure?
questions.correct_answer: ERC-1155, because it tracks balances by both address and token ID and can support multiple fungible or non-fungible item types.
incorrect_answers: ERC-20, because it registers unique token identifiers per account and can handle mixed metadata configurations in a single contract.
ERC-721, because it optimizes memory storage for gas savings and allows multiple identical items to share a single owner balance.
ERC-998, because it allows nested tokens within a parent contract and eliminates the need for separate metadata and balance indexing.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats standards as architectural commitments. ERC-1155 is suited to multi-token systems because balances are tracked per address and ID pair, unlike ERC-20's fungible balances or ERC-721's one-owner-per-token-ID model.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson warn that choosing a token standard is not merely a cosmetic implementation detail?
questions.correct_answer: The standard affects transfer granularity, identity model, wallet support, marketplace compatibility, indexer behavior, and future application logic.
incorrect_answers: The standard determines transaction consensus ordering, block inclusion priority, gas price scaling, network latency, and base-layer security.
The standard establishes legal property definition, physical custody rights, intellectual property ownership, and off-chain dispute resolution.
The standard replaces internal smart contract logic, validator verification rules, compiler optimization levels, and node communication protocols.
questions.explanation: ERC standards coordinate technical and social expectations across contracts, wallets, markets, and indexers. That coordination shapes what later applications can safely assume about the token.

questions.question_stem: An NFT's `tokenURI` points to an ordinary HTTP URL controlled by the issuer. What is the main integrity concern?
questions.correct_answer: The token can remain on-chain while the metadata or media at that location changes, disappears, or becomes misleading.
incorrect_answers: The token ID stops being unique on-chain while the external server database remains desynchronized, slow, or offline.
The token history becomes private to the issuer while the HTTP protocol blocks, encrypts, or exposes secret account signatures.
The token bytecode stores the image file on-chain while the gas consumption scales, increases, or exceeds contract limits.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes token permanence from metadata integrity. A location-addressed URL depends on a mutable server location, while content addressing provides stronger evidence that the referenced content has not changed.

questions.question_stem: A token-gated Discord checks wallet ownership before letting users enter a channel. What does the token gate actually enforce in this setup?
questions.correct_answer: It can condition access on current wallet ownership, while moderation, culture, server availability, and content hosting remain off-chain systems.
incorrect_answers: It can decentralize Discord's underlying server architecture, while user profiles, message routing, data storage, and chat histories remain centralized.
It can guarantee legal identity verification of every member, while sovereign law enforcement, court disputes, and citizen tracking remain off-chain systems.
It can enforce honest governance participation among all holders, while treasury execution, voting rules, and proposal submission remain off-chain systems.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents token communities as two-layer systems. The ownership check may be on-chain or wallet-based, but the community experience usually depends on social and operational infrastructure outside Ethereum.

questions.question_stem: A project uses an NFT as a membership badge and a fungible token to vote on treasury spending. How should a student classify this design?
questions.correct_answer: It is a hybrid token-community design where access or identity and governance power are handled by different token patterns.
incorrect_answers: It is a standard non-DAO structure where membership access and financial transactions must be authorized by a single multisig contract.
It is a centralized DAO architecture where all membership rights and treasury assets are held in escrow by a single validator address.
It is a fully decentralized system where dual standards prevent all sybil identities and strategic voter collusion.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats DAOs, membership NFTs, and social tokens as patterns that can be combined. The important question is what each token controls, not which brand label the community uses.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_06-EF-token_based_communities_and_nfts_in_practice-slides-only.qmd: Three Patterns: DAOs, Membership NFTs, and Social Tokens / Community Patterns And Hybrid Designs

questions.question_stem: A public mint lets anyone call `mint()` until the supply cap is reached. Why does the lesson treat minting as a distribution-policy decision, not just token creation?
questions.correct_answer: The mint logic decides initial ownership and can shape scarcity, fairness, bot exposure, payments, allowlists, signatures, and operator power.
incorrect_answers: The mint process only updates external metadata and cannot affect token ownership, transfer limits, contract state, or cumulative supply.
The mint execution requires manual validator approval and must verify legal identities, credit scores, KYC status, and physical address.
The mint interface is automatically configured by standard choices and cannot alter gas consumption, wallet compatibility, or minting price.
questions.explanation: Minting is a state-writing transaction that creates a token ID or balance and assigns an initial owner. Contract rules at that moment encode economic and governance choices.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_06-EF-token_based_communities_and_nfts_in_practice-slides-only.qmd: What Is Minting? / Minting on Ethereum / Minting And Distribution Policy

questions.question_stem: A marketplace reads an NFT royalty field but chooses not to pay royalties on resale. Which conclusion best matches the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Royalty metadata can signal creator payment expectations, but payment may still depend on marketplace enforcement and surrounding off-chain norms.
incorrect_answers: Royalty enforcement is handled by Ethereum consensus, but resales only fail when creator wallets cannot cover network gas fee costs.
Royalty smart contracts can automatically reverse secondary transfers, but executing the recovery depends on creator access to the market interface.
Royalty metadata can guarantee legal ownership and usage rights, but enforcing the physical copyrights depends entirely on cryptographic signatures alone.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses royalty signaling to reinforce the enforced-versus-signaled distinction. A standard can communicate expectations to marketplaces without guaranteeing every downstream venue enforces them.

questions.question_stem: In the DAO re-entrancy case, why did the exploit work even though Ethereum consensus and cryptography were functioning?
questions.correct_answer: The contract sent ETH before updating internal balances, allowing recursive withdrawals before the state reflected the first withdrawal.
incorrect_answers: The validators accepted invalid cryptographic signatures, allowing unauthorized asset transfers before the protocol could verify private keys.
The standard limited token transfers to once per block, allowing rapid flash loan manipulations before the contract could update its price oracle.
The consensus mechanism rewrote contract storage variables, allowing random state changes before the block header completed execution.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the DAO attack as a smart-contract sequencing failure. The chain faithfully executed vulnerable logic; checks-effects-interactions is one way to avoid that ordering bug.

questions.question_stem: A dApp stops working for most users because its main RPC provider has an outage, but Ethereum L1 continues producing blocks. What lesson concept does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Decentralized base-layer consensus can coexist with centralized operational chokepoints in RPC access, bridges, or oracles.
incorrect_answers: Any RPC outage means Ethereum L1 consensus has accepted an invalid state transition or finalized a corrupted block.
RPC configurations are defined inside the ERC-721 specification, making all non-fungible assets invalid during network failures.
Active base-layer block execution guarantees that all external bridges, oracles, and decentralized web interfaces remain accessible.
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by separating Ethereum L1 from service layers built above it. Analysts should evaluate concentrated infrastructure dependencies even when the base chain remains healthy.

questions.question_stem: In the assigned reading, how could soulbound tokens improve NFT provenance without proving off-chain truth by themselves?
questions.correct_answer: They can attach works to an issuing Soul's reputation, affiliations, and prior attestations, giving buyers social context to evaluate authenticity.
incorrect_answers: They can encrypt every digital image file across standard web servers, giving content creators absolute protection against unapproved replication.
They can compel international courts and galleries to accept the token, giving buyers legally binding property deeds that eliminate disputes.
They can remove the need to trust credential authorities, giving communities immune networks where fraudulent issuance is impossible.
questions.explanation: The reading's claim is narrower than automatic truth. SBTs can add verifiable social context and issuer reputation, but credibility, revocation, and off-chain interpretation still matter.

questions.question_stem: Two DAO votes have the same number of supporting wallets. In one vote, most supporters share the same issuer attestations and affiliations; in the other, supporters come from socially distant communities. What reading mechanism addresses this difference?
questions.correct_answer: Correlation-aware governance can discount highly correlated Souls because shared SBT patterns may indicate sybils, collusion, common bias, or over-coordination.
incorrect_answers: One-token-one-vote mechanics can mathematically resolve the disparity because capital concentrations accurately measure social pluralism and voter diversity.
Targeted souldrop operations can privilege highly correlated voter profiles because redundant credentials confirm genuine alignment and community consensus.
Standard Nakamoto coefficients can determine social distance because simple address counts reliably reveal voter independence, diversity, and community separation.
questions.explanation: The reading argues that decentralization cannot be measured only by wallet counts or token balances. Shared SBTs can reveal correlation, and governance can try to reward cooperation across social distance.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/desoc.txt: DAO Governance And Decentralization / Correlation discounting

questions.question_stem: A platform proposes making all education, employment, and membership SBTs public so anyone can verify credentials. What is the strongest reading-based concern?
questions.correct_answer: Public credentials can aid verification, but they can also expose sensitive affiliations and enable discrimination, coercive access controls, or social-credit dynamics.
incorrect_answers: Public metadata systems can eliminate sybil identities entirely, but managing individual user privacy remains a simple interface preference rather than a core design tradeoff.
Private attestation frameworks can secure personal reputation graphs, but measuring decentralization or detecting collusion requires fully transparent voter affiliations.
Non-transferable credentials can prevent token sales on secondary markets, but verifying identity and enforcing honest participation requires offline physical audits.
questions.explanation: The reading treats privacy and publicity as a structural tradeoff. Some visibility supports provenance and sybil resistance, but too much visibility can turn social trust infrastructure into surveillance and exclusion infrastructure.
